raw_response.headline_result_summary: Using retrospective life-history data (EMIUB 2000) and Cox proportional hazard models for individuals in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, the study finds a nuanced, zone-contingent relationship between housing tenure (residence status), formal urban zoning, and sustained household piped water (PW) access. On the paper's headline tenure variable (Residence status, with Owner/co-owner as reference), results are substantively mixed across transitions, urban zones, and specifications because households frequently leave equipped rental housing to buy affordable plots in unserviced peripheral/non-zoned areas: tenants are significantly more likely than owners to gain first PW access overall (Model 1a HR = 2.56, p < 0.001) and in the zoned periphery (Model 1b/Table 4 HR = 2.94, p < 0.01), do not differ from owners downtown (HR = 0.88, n.s.), and are less likely than owners to gain PW in the non-zoned periphery (HR = 0.00, p < 0.001). For losing PW, tenants appear at lower risk than owners when zone is omitted (Model 2a HR = 0.53, p < 0.001), but controlling for zone reverses this pattern: tenant vs. owner loss risk is elevated though statistically non-significant at p < 0.05 in downtown (HR = 1.67, p < 0.15) and zoned periphery (HR = 1.43, p < 0.15) and significantly higher for renters in the non-zoned periphery (HR = 6.31, p < 0.01). By contrast, formal urban land zoning (Zone of residence) is unambiguously favorable to access: compared with the zoned periphery, living in the non-zoned (informal/unallocated) periphery sharply reduces the hazard of gaining PW (HR = 0.14, p < 0.001 among owners; 0.00, p < 0.001 among renters) and dramatically increases the hazard of losing PW (HR = 15.38 to 68.00, p < 0.001), as utility connections are not permitted in non-zoned areas. Formal-sector employment increases the hazard of gaining PW (HR = 2.61–3.03, p < 0.001) but is null for losing PW (HR = 1.04 and 0.78, n.s.).
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls: Five major coding pitfalls exist in this paper: (1) EXPOSURE SELECTION (HOUSING TENURE VS. URBAN ZONING): Housing tenure (Owner vs. Renter) is the paper's primary headline focus in the Abstract and Discussion and exhibits a genuinely mixed, trade-off pattern, whereas formal urban land zoning (Zoned periphery / Downtown vs. Non-zoned periphery) is consistently and strongly favorable to piped water access (non-zoned periphery is strongly unfavorable). Any synthesis coding must distinguish whether the extracted exposure is individual property ownership/tenure or municipal zoning/land formalization. (2) REFERENCE CATEGORY ORIENTATION FOR TENURE: Owner/co-owner is the omitted reference category (= 1), and Renting/co-renting is the reported dummy. A HR > 1 on Renting in Table 2 (HR = 2.56***) means renting is associated with BETTER first access—and therefore homeownership is associated with WORSE first access. (3) OPPOSITE OUTCOME POLARITY BETWEEN TABLE 2 AND TABLE 5: Table 2 (and Tables 3–4) models first GAIN of piped water (HR > 1 = better access), whereas Table 5 (and Tables 6–7) models first LOSS of piped water (HR > 1 = worse sustained access / faster loss). (4) CONFOUNDING / SIGN REVERSAL BETWEEN MODEL 2a AND MODEL 2b: In Table 5 (first loss of PW), omitting zone of residence (Model 2a) gives Renting HR = 0.53*** (lower loss risk for renters because people move into newly acquired unserviced homes to become owners), whereas adding zone of residence and interactions (Model 2b / Table 7) flips Renting vs. Owner to HR = 1.43 (p < 0.15) in zoned periphery, HR = 1.67 (p < 0.15) downtown, and HR = 6.31** in non-zoned periphery. (5) UNCONVENTIONAL p < 0.15 SUPERSCRIPT ('d'): All tables flag p < 0.15 with superscript 'd' (e.g., Renting HR = 1.43^d in Table 5/7 and 1.67^d in Table 7). The text on PDF p. 14 describes tenants as having 'a greater risk of losing PW' downtown and in the zoned periphery based on Table 7, even though neither estimate reaches conventional p < 0.05 (or even p < 0.10) significance. Note also minor sample-size discrepancy for the loss analysis between Table 1 (1,226 persons at risk) and text on PDF p. 12 (1,220 people).
raw_response.study_design: Retrospective life-course event history analysis using semi-parametric Cox proportional hazard models with time-varying covariates (from a nationally representative two-stage stratified retrospective survey, EMIUB 2000)
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Individuals aged 15–64 who ever resided in Ouagadougou (total ever at risk = 3,133: 2,839 interviewed in Ouagadougou and 294 interviewed elsewhere in Burkina Faso). Analytic risk sets: First access to piped water N = 2,134 individuals (232 events; 255,057 person-time units); First loss of piped water N = 1,226 individuals in Table 1 / 1,220 reported in text on PDF p. 12 (294 events; 103,963 person-time units); Descriptive residential sequences N = 2,839 individuals interviewed in Ouagadougou.
